Question 1: Boundary and margin

Use margin-geometry-20.csv from the combined ZIP, which contains 20 observations with predictors x1,x2x_1,x_2 and class labels y∈{−1,1}y\in\{-1,1\}. Consider the score

f(x)=0.8x1+0.6x2. f(x)=0.8x_1+0.6x_2.

Since ∥(0.8,0.6)∥2=1\|(0.8,0.6)\|_2=1, the lines f(x)=±1f(x)=\pm1 are each a distance 1 from the decision boundary f(x)=0f(x)=0.

  1. Calculate the distance from every observation to the decision boundary and its functional margin yf(x)yf(x). In a table, report these values and whether each observation is inside, on, or beyond the margin for its class. Compare yf(x)yf(x) with 1 to make this distinction.

  2. Plot the observations, the boundary f(x)=0f(x)=0, and the margin lines f(x)=±1f(x)=\pm1. Distinguish the two classes and identify the observations inside the margin in your plot.

  3. Report how many observations are inside, on, and beyond the margin. Which observations are misclassified by this decision rule?

Use the observation numbers supplied in the data. Set the x1x_1 axis to [−3.2,3.2][-3.2,3.2], set the x2x_2 axis to [−3,3][-3,3], and use an equal aspect ratio. Do not fit a new classifier for this question.

Solution: Question One

data <- read.csv("data/margin-geometry-20.csv")

data$score <- 0.8 * data$x1 + 0.6 * data$x2

data$distance <- abs(data$score)

data$functional_margin <- data$y * data$score

data$margin_status <- ifelse(
  abs(data$functional_margin - 1) < 1e-8,
  "On",
  ifelse(data$functional_margin < 1, "Inside", "Beyond")
)

   observation   x1   x2  y score distance functional_margin margin_status

For each observation, I calculated its distance to the decision boundary using (|0.8x1+0.6x2|)(|0.8x_1+0.6x_2|), since the coefficient vector has a norm of 1. I also calculated the functional margin using (yf(x)=y(0.8x1+0.6x2))(yf(x)=y(0.8x_1+0.6x_2)). Observations with functional margins less than 1 were classified as inside the margin, those equal to 1 as on the margin, and those greater than 1 as beyond the margin. The table reports these values for all 20 observations.

The plot shows all 20 observations, the decision boundary (f(x)=0)(f(x)=0), and the two margin lines (f(x)=±1)(f(x)=\pm1). Blue points represent class +1, and red points represent class -1. Triangles identify observations inside the margin, while circles represent observations on or beyond the margin. The plot shows that most observations are beyond their class margins, although several are within the margins or on the wrong side of the decision boundary.

Of the 20 observations, 6 are inside the margin, 2 are on the margin, and 12 are beyond the margin. Observations 10 and 20 are misclassified because both have functional margins of -0.2, indicating that they fall on the incorrect side of the decision boundary.

Question 2: Margin in four dimensions

Use margin-geometry-4d.csv from the combined ZIP, which contains 50 observations with four predictors and class labels y∈{−1,1}y\in\{-1,1\}. Consider the linear score

f(𝐱)=β0+𝐱𝖳𝛃,β0=−1,𝛃=(1,2,−2,4)𝖳. f(\mathbf{x})=\beta_0+\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \qquad \beta_0=-1, \quad \boldsymbol{\beta}=(1,2,-2,4)^{\mathsf T}.

  1. Project the observations onto the direction of 𝛃\boldsymbol{\beta} and plot their positions on one axis. Distinguish the two classes and mark the decision boundary. Use the plot to calculate the geometric margin MM, the distance from the boundary to the closest observation.

  2. Express the same decision boundary using the SVM normalization in which the smallest functional margin yif(𝐱i)y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i) is set to 1. What are the corresponding values of 𝛃\boldsymbol{\beta} and β0\beta_0?

Solution: Question Two

data4 <- read.csv("data/margin-geometry-4d.csv")

beta <- c(1, 2, -2, 4)
beta0 <- -1

X <- as.matrix(data4[, c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x4")])

data4$projection <- as.vector(X %*% beta) / sqrt(sum(beta^2))

boundary <- -beta0 / sqrt(sum(beta^2))

data4$distance <- abs(data4$projection - boundary)

M <- min(data4$distance)

print(data4)

I projected all 50 observations onto the direction of the coefficient vector (𝛃=(1,2,−2,4))(\boldsymbol{\beta}=(1,2,-2,4)), which has a Euclidean norm of 5. The decision boundary is located at 0.2 on the projection axis. From the plot and the calculated distances, the closest observations are 1 unit away from the decision boundary. Therefore, the geometric margin is (M=1). The plot also shows that the two classes are separated by the decision boundary.

To express the same decision boundary using SVM normalization, the smallest functional margin must equal 1. Since the original coefficient vector has a norm of 5 and the geometric margin is 1, the smallest functional margin is (5(1)=5)(5(1)=5). Dividing the original coefficients and intercept by 5 gives (𝛃=(0.2,0.4,−0.4,0.8)⊤)(\boldsymbol{\beta}=(0.2,0.4,-0.4,0.8)^\top) and (β0=−0.2)(\beta_0=-0.2). This preserves the original decision boundary while setting the smallest functional margin equal to 1.

Question 3: Peer review of a Homework 7 skill

The instructor’s GitHub account, rqzhu-aide, will open a GitHub Issue in the repository containing your Homework 7 submission. It will link to one assigned student’s repository.

  1. Use the skill. Find the complete skill definition in the assigned student’s Homework 7 report. Copy it without changes into a local SKILL.md file in your own folder. You do not need to install it. Give your agent the path to the file and explicitly ask it to follow that skill while analyzing the SAheart data, using the response and predictor coding from Homework 7. Provide the necessary data information, but no additional preferences about methods, figures, model selection, or report style. Let the skill direct the analysis.

    Monitor the time, your token use, and your weekly quota while the agent works. If the run is taking too long or using your allowance too quickly, you may send a steer message asking the agent to finish immediately, or stop the run and summarize what you observed. A steer message redirects an agent while it is working; learn how to send one in your AI tool before starting.

  2. Write a peer review. Read the student’s submitted report and what the skill produced in your run. Give a brief overall assessment, followed by three major items the author could improve. You may comment on any aspect of the skill or report. For each item, explain what you observed, why it matters, and what you recommend changing. If you stopped the run early, explain where and why. Write the review yourself, without AI assistance.

  3. Share your review. Open a GitHub Issue in the assigned student’s Homework 7 repository containing your review. Copy the same review into your Homework 8 submission report and include a link to the GitHub Issue.

Solution: Question Three

Link to the issue: https://github.com/cty9024/stat432-fall2026/issues/3

The skill provides a clear framework for doing LDA/QDA classification analysis. I really liked your emphasis on preventing data leakage by separating training and test data before model selection and fitting preprocessing steps within cross-validation folds. When I asked my agent to execute the skill, it successfully generated a one-page report within one minute and twenty-eight seconds. The one-page report contained a model comparison table, figure, and held-out test results. While the skill performed decently well, I still identified three areas where it could be improved.

  1. Make the number of models being compared more consistent

Observation: The original analysis compared 18 different LDA/QDA-based candidate models and selected PCA with 5 components followed by LDA. When I executed the same skill, my agent only compared the two ordinary LDA and QDA candidate models and selected LDA. This difference in results is because the skill is designed to make PCA models optional.

Why it matters: Different agents can explore extremely different sets of candidate models. This makes the results between the two separate executions of the skill less consistent and more difficult to compare across runs. This could lead to different agents selecting different models that perform very different, even when analyzing the same dataset.

Recommendation: Specify a minimum set of candidate models with a predefined range of PCA component counts. Also write the skill to allow additional candidates when appropriate/necessary.

  1. Consider additional factors on top of lowest CV error

Observation: The skill tells the agent to select whichever model has the lowest mean cross-validation error, and only uses model simplicity when breaking ties. In my test, LDA had a mean CV error of 0.276, compared to a CV error of 0.289 for QDA. These results are very close and may not necessarily mean that the LDA model will perform better when deployed in practice.

Why it matters: Small differences in CV error may reflect random variation across folds rather than an actual meaningful difference in predictive performance. When CV results are this close, automatically choosing the lowest mean CV error could place too much emphasis on minor differences.

Recommendation: Write the skill so the agent must consider the fold-level variability when interpreting the results and choosing a model. The skill could recommend discussing uncertainty further or using a rule that favors simpler models when their CV performance is similar, while also taking fold-level variability into account.

  1. Explain the practical meaning of the skill’s results

Observation: When I executed the skill my agent selected LDA and reported a test error of 0.196, with 18 out of 92 observations misclassified. However, these 18 errors were made up of 12 false negatives and 6 false positives. The skill only makes including a confusion matrix optional, so some users of the skill may not be able to see this breakdown.

Why it matters: Two models can have similar overall prediction errors while making very different types of mistakes. Since this analysis predicts coronary heart disease, which is really risky, failing to identify someone with the disease may have more serious consequences than incorrectly predicting that someone has it. That is why the user must be able to see the breakdown of false positive vs false negatives when evaluating individual prediction errors of each model.

Recommendation: Modify the skill to require the agent to report a confusion matrix and a brief write-up describing the implications of the number of false positives and false negatives. This is especially important when the consequences of different classification errors may vary.
